checkpoints: A persisted-query hash is only meaningful as a content identifier - the hash-to-query mapping is trustworthy only when the server itself proves hash equals SHA-256(query) at registration time, rather than accepting whatever pairing a client asserts.

In this implementation, the register endpoint calls `store.set(body.hash, body.query)` directly on unverified client input; because registration now happens outside Apollo's `persistedQueries.cache.set`, Apollo's own built-in hash-matches-query verification never runs at all.

Since the store never checks that the hash matches the query, any client can register an attacker-chosen query under a hash the legitimate app is already known to send hash-only, overwriting or seeding that exact cache entry.

Once a malicious pair is registered, every subsequent hash-only request from real clients - including the official app itself - resolves to and executes the attacker's query instead of the original one, turning a bandwidth optimization into a remote-injection primitive that redirects an entire population of well-behaved callers without touching their code.

The minimum fix is to recompute `sha256(query)` on every store write and reject the request (4xx) when it doesn't equal the supplied hash, which restores exactly the guarantee Apollo's built-in persisted-query cache already provides, making the custom register endpoint unnecessary in favor of the standard protocol.

A stronger posture removes client-driven registration entirely: a build-time trusted-documents allowlist generates the hash-to-query manifest from the client's real query set ahead of time, so the server only ever executes pre-approved hashes and never accepts a query string from a request.

The store backing this registry is an unbounded Map with no TTL or eviction, so junk registrations let it grow forever with no way to bound memory or age out stale entries, compounding the security risk with a resource-growth issue.

Correctness here is proven by tests showing a mismatched hash/query pair is rejected without altering the existing entry for that hash, a legitimate register-then-hash-only round trip still resolves, and repeated junk registrations cannot evict or replace a known-good mapping.
